cards.explanation: The word is keep. The writer says, “save me, that I may keep Your testimonies.” He wants the rescue, and he wants to keep God's testimonies once he has it. I think that's a man who plans to stay put on the right path, not just get out of the mess.

The answer is in God's word. The writer says, “in Your word I have put my hope.” Notice what he's doing before dawn: he's up and crying for help. And right there in the same verse, his hope sits in the word.

The answer is to meditate on God's word. He says his eyes anticipate the watches of night, “…that I may meditate on Your word.” So the night isn't just something he stays up through. He looks ahead to it because he wants that time with the word. I think that's a man who wants more hours with God's word, not fewer.

The answer is False. The people who follow after wickedness draw near to the writer, but verse 150 says they “…are far from Your law.” They're close in one direction and far in the other. That's some very impressive distance management, friends.

The word is true. The writer says, “You are near, O LORD, and all Your commandments are true.” Notice he says it right when the wicked are drawing near. He sets that next to the fact that God is near. I think that's a man who knows where to look when the crowd gets close.
The answer is False. Verse 152 says, “Long ago I learned from Your testimonies that You have established them forever.” That's not last week's news. He's been standing on this one for a long time.

The reason he gives is that he has not forgotten God's law. He says, “Look upon my affliction and rescue me, for I have not forgotten Your law.” He doesn't list his good deeds or his history. He just says he hasn't forgotten the law.

The answer is True. The writer says, “Salvation is far from the wicked because they do not seek Your statutes.” Pay attention to the reason he gives. It's the not seeking. Earlier he says, “in Your word I have put my hope.” (Psalm 119:147), so I think he's showing us the other side of that.

The answer is False. The writer says, “Though my persecutors and foes are many, I have not turned from Your testimonies.” That word though matters. Lots of people against him, and he doesn't turn. It would be easy to say they'd wear him down, but the verse says otherwise.

He asks the LORD to consider how he loves God's precepts. He says, “Consider how I love Your precepts, O LORD; give me life according to Your loving devotion.” He points to his love for the precepts. Then he asks for life according to God's loving devotion.
The answer is all of it. Verse 160 says, “The entirety of Your word is truth…” Entirety means the whole thing. Not a favorite chapter or a few good verses. He means every bit of it.

The word is word. The writer says, “Rulers persecute me without cause, but my heart fears only Your word.” Rulers are on one side, and God's word is on the other. His heart has only one thing it fears.

The picture is someone who finds great spoil. The writer says, “I rejoice in Your promise like one who finds great spoil.” That's a joy you can picture, someone coming across a big find. The comparison is for his rejoicing in God's promise.

The answer is seven. Verse 164 says, “Seven times a day I praise You for Your righteous judgments.” That's a lot of praise in one day. I'm out here with flour on my mustache and I can't keep up with that.

The answer is False. Verse 165 says, “Abundant peace belongs to those who love Your law; nothing can make them stumble.” Not a small thing, not a medium thing, nothing. It's right there next to the abundant peace.

The answer is True. The writer says, “I obey Your precepts and Your testimonies, for all my ways are before You.” The word for ties the obeying to his ways being before God. I think that's a man who knows he's never out of God's sight, and he lives like it.

The answer is understanding. The writer says, “May my cry come before You, O LORD; give me understanding according to Your word.” He's not asking for a pile of stuff. He wants to understand, and he wants it according to God's word.

The answer is True. Verse 171 says, “My lips pour forth praise, for You teach me Your statutes.” The praise pours out, and God's teaching is the reason he gives. I'd say a lot of us would love a mouth like that on a Monday morning.

The word is chosen. The writer says, “May Your hand be ready to help me, for I have chosen Your precepts.” He didn't just land on them. He chose them, and that's the reason he gives for asking for help.
The answer is to praise God. Verse 175 says, “Let me live to praise You; may Your judgments sustain me.” He wants to live so that he can praise. Praise is the reason he gives for asking to live.

The answer is that he has strayed like a lost sheep. The psalm ends, “I have strayed like a lost sheep; seek Your servant, for I have not forgotten Your commandments.” He says it plainly about himself. And then he asks to be sought.
